Last thing, three small helpers that the wallet and trading skills need:

You do not have to memorise these. The agent picks the right one on its own.
    This is so you know what you can ask for.
Works out what a mint really is
Finds the real contract, the real price, whether the mint is actually open, and which network it is on. The one that stops you getting scammed by a fake price.
Mints from many wallets at once
For drops that sell out in seconds. Creates the wallets, tells you exactly how much to put in each, and fires them the moment the mint opens.
Prices up buying a whole floor
Adds up every cheap listing in a collection and gives you the real total before you buy them all.
For pages offering a free mint, a refund or an airdrop. It figures out what the site is really doing before you connect a wallet.
Scores every NFT and puts them in order using the same maths OpenSea uses, so the ranks match. It can catch a reveal before OpenSea updates itself.
After a reveal, finds the rarest items listed at normal floor prices and buys them before anyone notices.
Buys a listed NFT for you
Buys from the resale market, always testing the purchase first so a broken order never costs you a fee.
Checks if the buyers were real
Looks at who minted and tells you whether they were real people or a few wallets faking interest to look popular.
When a project says "we did X", this checks the blockchain to see if it is true.
Floors, sales, holders, how fast things flip. What the numbers actually say.
What it is worth, what can go wrong after you buy, and whether the price makes sense for the risk.
Rules for taking profit instead of holding forever. The boring one that saves the most money.
Makes new wallets, backs the keys up properly, and moves tokens without ever exposing them.
Follows specific wallets and pings you when they buy something.
Takes a list of wallets and hands you a clean, shareable spreadsheet.
Links anonymous handles and wallets that belong to the same person.
The art plan, the traits, the pricing, the mint page and the contract mechanics, all in one place.
Keeps every attribute consistent and grouped so your metadata does not turn into a mess.
Audits each trait for duplicates and anything that looks wrong before you launch.
Pulls on-chain data without paying for an API. The engine under a lot of the others.
A local dashboard for minting: plan a mint, rehearse it, manage a set of wallets, watch the floor, and see what happened afterwards.
A read-only screen of upcoming mints and market movement, noting where every number came from.
Hashcats, FAB4200 and others like them give you the item for finding a lucky number instead of paying. This runs that search for you.
Runs that search on your machine or on rented hardware, with checking so it never wastes a transaction.
Solves mints that make you think
Riddles and hidden clues that gate some drops, found by reading the game's own code.
Takes an on-chain game apart to show where value comes from.
Checks what the betting markets are pricing for an event.
Background research on Proof of Play and Pirate Nation.
Lets an agent prove who it is when it posts online, so a real one can be told from a fake.
How to give an agent its own account and have it post without leaking anything private.
Notes for a different blockchain, the Internet Computer.
No matching skills. Try a different term or category.

Some drops do not have a price. Instead of paying, you have to find a lucky
    number, and whoever finds one first gets the cat. That is what people mean when
    they say a mint is solved rather than bought.

Your laptop can do it, but it would take days, and people with big rented
    computers find them in minutes. So you rent one for a few minutes. That is the
    only reason for any of this.
Rent a computer for a few minutes (free to start)

rents computers by the second. You do not buy anything. You sign up

    will probably never pay anything.

This is the entire operation. Mention your bot and paste this:
It reports the round back to you. When you want to actually go for it:
@yourbot go ahead and mine the current round. stop when you find one, or after 15 minutes
And to see how it went:
@yourbot did we get one? show me the transaction
It checks the whole setup first, so a run never starts out broken
It does the searching on the rented computer, not yours
It checks every answer before spending anything, so one that arrived too late never costs you a fee
It sends the transaction from your wallet and gives you the link
The two things only you can do
Put a little ETH in your wallet.
Winning still costs a few cents in fees. Nothing can do that part for you.
Rounds move on constantly, and work done for a round that has already ended is wasted. Short and frequent beats one long run.

You are racing everyone else trying the same
    drop, and you pay for the computing whether you win or lose. That is what the
    free credit is for. Use it, keep your attempts short, and do not top up
    expecting a guaranteed cat.
Same idea and the same kind of prompt. You just name the one you want instead:
@yourbot use pow-mint-mining on FAB4200. what would a full attempt cost me, and is it worth it at today's difficulty?
There is no special wording, but sharper questions get sharper answers.
Paste a link and say what you want.

Give it the contract, not the name.
    Tell it your budget. Tell it when to stop. Ask for the number that decides it.
Paste a tweet that says "mint this"

This is the useful one. Drop the tweet in and it works out what the mint is,
    what it really costs, whether it is still open, and whether the project looks
    real, before anything touches your wallet.

It will not just fire off a transaction. It reads the tweet, finds the
    contract, checks the price and the supply on-chain, shows you what it found,
    and waits for you to say go.
